title: You Can Lead a Horse to Water…
author: Claudia Lewis
summary: Claudia Lewis uses a TikTok dance trend as an extended analogy for passive versus active learning: after watching around 70 videos of the 'Molly Long dance,' she found she could only perform about two-thirds of it, because watching wasn't the same as engaging her brain to actually learn the sequence. She argues the same failure mode happens constantly in classrooms -- students sit passively, copying notes and 'listening nicely,' assuming familiarity will translate into knowledge, when in fact passive exposure produces only a vague sense of recognition rather than usable understanding. Her fix, both for learning the dance and for teaching quantitative chemistry to a Year 10 class, is chunking: break the larger process into small pieces, check each piece before moving on, then combine and practice with increasing challenge -- for the chemistry example, isolating Mr, then the concept of a mole, before ever combining them into the full n = m/Mr calculation. She closes with a practical revision implication: because familiarity feels like knowledge but isn't, students assessing their own revision should answer real questions rather than passively highlighting or color-coding notes, since it's much harder to fool yourself about what you know when you're actually getting questions wrong.
points: Lewis's self-experiment (about 70 viewings of a dance video, only two-thirds of the steps actually retrievable) gives a concrete, relatable demonstration of the gap between passive exposure and active learning that mirrors student self-assessment errors.

Her classroom application chunks a multi-step chemistry calculation (n = m/Mr) into isolated, individually-checked components -- Mr first, then the concept of a mole, only then the combined formula -- directly operationalizing the chunking principle from the dance analogy.

Lewis names the mechanism explicitly: mini-whiteboards and cold call function as forced engagement tools, making it 'too difficult to be a passive learner when you are constantly being asked to do something.'

Her revision advice -- answer real questions rather than color-code or highlight notes -- targets the same underlying failure (familiarity mistaken for knowledge) in a self-study context rather than a live classroom one.
quotes: Too often, I encounter students who believe they can simply sit, passively in a lesson and absorb what is being taught, without having to do anything.
I didn’t watch them to learn. I hadn’t put my brain in gear, I hadn’t engaged what needed to be engaged in order to learn it.
We have to force our students to put their brains into gear, we have to depress the clutch if you will.
Rather than jumping in with moles = mass ÷ relative formula mass, first we looked at Mr. We checked we could do that, then we looked at the concept of a mole and we checked we could do that.
By demanding, by expecting and sanctioning as appropriate, student participation in my lesson, I am making it more likely that they will get into gear and put their brain in learning mode.

When it comes to revision, when it comes to them assessing whether they know and understand something, get them answering questions rather than highlighting things. It's much harder to lie to yourself and convince yourself you know something when you're getting the questions wrong.
